newsitem.title: USA: Mexico decertification bill cleared for U.S. House.
newsitem.headline: Mexico decertification bill cleared for U.S. House.

text.p: The U.S. House of Representatives Rules Committee on Wednesday cleared for action by the full House a bill to overturn President Bill Clinton's finding that Mexico is fully cooperating in the anti-drug war.

The committee's action cleared the way for a vote by the House on Thursday. The bill, approved by the House International Relations Committee last week, would waive the sanctions against Mexico required by U.S. law for countries that are not certified as a U.S. ally in the drugs war.
Clinton certified Mexico on Feb. 28 as a fully cooperating partner in the drug war despite objections of many members of Congress.

The Rules Committee made in order a vote on an amendment to the bill that would delay decertification by 90 days to give Mexico time to meet six conditions to permit certification. These include allowing U.S. drug agents in Mexico to carry weapons and giving assurances that it will extradite drug cartel members to the United States.
The White House says Clinton would veto the legislation as it now stands if it passes both the House and Senate. A two-thirds majority is required in both chambers to override a presidential veto.

Under a 1961 law, congressional disapproval of Clinton's certification that Mexico is an anti-drug ally automatically triggers a ban on U.S. aid and requires votes against multilateral development bank assistance to Mexico.
